steelGrades.name: Austenitic AISI 304 (18/10 Culinary Stainless Steel)
steelGrades.composition: 18% Chromium, 10% Nickel, 0.08% Carbon, 2% Manganese, Balance Iron
steelGrades.acidResistance: High (Dense Cr2O3 passive barrier; vulnerable during first 3 cook cycles or prolonged acidic boils)
steelGrades.fdaEuCompliance: Fully Compliant with Council of Europe Resolution CM/Res(2013)9 and US FDA GRAS
steelGrades.description: The quintessential culinary workhorse found in premium tri-ply cookware (All-Clad, Demeyere, Le Creuset, Calphalon). Contains 18% chromium, which spontaneously reacts with oxygen to form a nanometer-thin passivating chromium(III) oxide (Cr2O3) layer. While virtually impervious to neutral foods, hot organic acids (citric, malic, acetic at pH < 4.0) cause slow passive dissolution, releasing measurable nickel and chromium ions into simmering sauces, especially when cookware is brand new.

steelGrades.name: Marine & Surgical Grade AISI 316 (18/10/2.5 Mo)
steelGrades.acidResistance: Exceptional / Surgical Grade (Molybdenum suppresses chloride pitting and organic acid chelation)
steelGrades.fdaEuCompliance: Highest Safety Tier under CM/Res(2013)9; Exceeds all global food contact benchmarks
steelGrades.description: Engineered for harsh chemical reactors, marine hardware, and high-end surgical cookware (e.g. 316Ti / Heritage Steel). The addition of 2.0% to 3.0% molybdenum (Mo) forms an ultra-dense, self-healing oxy-molybdate surface film. This elevates the Pitting Resistance Equivalent Number (PREN) from 18 to over 25, reducing nickel and chromium leaching by 75% to 85% compared to standard 304 steel during long acidic tomato and vinegar reductions.

steelGrades.name: Ferritic AISI 430 (18/0 Magnetic Nickel-Free Steel)
steelGrades.composition: 16-18% Chromium, <0.5% Nickel, 0% Molybdenum, 0.12% Carbon, Balance Iron
steelGrades.acidResistance: Moderate (Zero nickel hazard; slightly higher chromium release in long intense acid boils)
steelGrades.fdaEuCompliance: Clinically Recommended for patients diagnosed with Systemic Nickel Allergy Syndrome (SNAS)
steelGrades.description: A ferritic, magnetic stainless alloy commonly used for exterior induction-clad layers, economy mixing bowls, and hypoallergenic cookware lines (Homichef, Cuisinart French Classic exterior). Because nickel content is negligible (<0.5%), it releases virtually zero nickel ions into food (<0.5 µg/kg), eliminating flare-up risks for nickel-sensitive individuals. However, lacking nickel's face-centered cubic stability, it has lower corrosion resistance under extreme boiling acidity.

steelGrades.name: Austenitic 200-Series (Manganese-Substituted Economy Steel)
steelGrades.acidResistance: Poor to Moderate (Low chromium; unstable passive film prone to intergranular attack)
steelGrades.fdaEuCompliance: Restricted in EU; flagged by food safety authorities for excessive manganese co-leaching
steelGrades.description: A low-cost formulation widely used in unbranded imported stockpots and cheap kitchenware. Manufacturers substitute high-priced nickel with industrial manganese (Mn) and nitrogen to preserve an austenitic crystal structure. The depleted chromium level weakens the Cr2O3 passive layer, accelerating acid attack in simmering tomato sauce and co-leaching substantial quantities of neurotoxic manganese alongside chromium and nickel.

steelGrades.name: High-Carbon Martensitic Stainless (AISI 440C / German DIN 1.4116 Blades)
steelGrades.composition: 14-17% Chromium, 0.95-1.20% Carbon, <0.6% Nickel, 0.75% Molybdenum, Balance Iron
steelGrades.acidResistance: Low in Acid Immersion (Chromium tied up as grain boundary carbides; prone to pitting)
steelGrades.fdaEuCompliance: Approved for brief slicing and food prep; strictly prohibited for boiling or liquid immersion
steelGrades.description: Tempered cutlery steel hardened to 56–60 HRC for razor-sharp chef knives. During thermal heat treatment, a substantial portion of chromium precipitates out as brittle chromium carbide (Cr23C6) micro-clusters along crystal boundaries, depleting free matrix chromium below the 12% passivation threshold ('sensitization'). If knives are submerged in acidic marinades or washed in alkaline dishwashers, aggressive pitting and chromium leaching occur rapidly.

steelGrades.name: Vitreous Silicate Enamel Clad (Le Creuset / Staub Reference)
steelGrades.composition: 100% Fused Borosilicate & Feldspar Glass Glaze bonded at 850°C
steelGrades.acidResistance: Complete Chemical Immunity (Vitreous glass impervious to organic acids up to pH 1.0)
steelGrades.fdaEuCompliance: Gold Standard Inert Reference; Zero metal migration across all food contact standards
steelGrades.description: The definitive non-reactive culinary benchmark. A non-porous layer of vitreous borosilicate glass enamel fused to a heavy metal core at 850°C. Completely insulates food from all underlying metal elements. Immune to acidic dissolution, chelation, and galvanic micro-pitting, ensuring 0.0 µg/kg leaching of nickel, chromium, and heavy metals regardless of simmering time or acidity.

panConditions.name: Brand-New / 1st to 3rd Cook Cycle (Unpassivated Grain Boundaries)
panConditions.description: Kamerud et al. (2013) published in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry showed that brand-new stainless steel pans release up to 6.8x more nickel and 8.5x more chromium during initial cooking cycles. Manufacturing abrasives, residual pickling reagents, and fresh unoxidized grain boundaries allow rapid ion chelation by organic acids. After 6 consecutive cook cycles, metal release drops exponentially to stable baseline levels.

panConditions.name: Fully Passivated / Mature Pan (>10 Cook Cycles, Intact Cr2O3 Film)
panConditions.passivationStatus: Optimal / Continuous 2-3 nm Cr2O3 Passive Barrier
panConditions.description: A seasoned, mature pan where repeated culinary heating and atmospheric oxygen exposure have formed a continuous, self-healing chromium(III) oxide (Cr2O3) ceramic shield across all microscopic crystal facets. Base leaching remains safely below European Resolution CM/Res(2013)9 Specific Release Limits under standard domestic cooking.

panConditions.name: Mechanically Scoured with Steel Wool / Abrasive Scour Pad
panConditions.description: Scrubbing burned food with heavy stainless steel wool or abrasive green pads physically scratches away the nanometer-thin Cr2O3 passive film, exposing bare unoxidized austenitic crystals. This creates an immediate 3x to 4x surge in heavy metal ion release during the next cooking cycle until the surface naturally re-passivates via thermal oxidation.

panConditions.name: Chloride Pitted (Cold Salting / Dishwasher Salt Attack)
panConditions.description: Salting water before it reaches a rolling boil causes dense NaCl salt crystals to sink and rest against the bottom of the pot. Highly concentrated chloride ions (Cl⁻) dissolve the protective passive oxide film, initiating localized micro-pitting. These microscopic pits harbor trapped acidic juices, establishing active galvanic corrosion cells that steadily release heavy metals into food.

foodMatrices.name: Slow-Simmered Tomato Marinara / Bolognese
foodMatrices.chelationPotency: High (Citric and malic acids act as bidentate and tridentate metal chelators)
foodMatrices.organolepticRisk: Sauce simmered >3 hrs in unpassivated steel can acquire a metallic off-taste (0.2+ mg/kg metal ions)
foodMatrices.description: The benchmark acid test for cookware metallurgy. Pureed tomatoes contain ~0.5% citric acid and ~0.1% malic acid at pH 3.8. At simmering temperatures of 95°C, carboxylate anions chemically bind and pull nickel and chromium ions directly from the stainless steel matrix, forming soluble metal-organic chelate complexes.

foodMatrices.name: Lemon Juice & Vinegar Gastrique / Glaze Reduction
foodMatrices.chelationPotency: Extreme (High hydronium [H+] ion concentration dissolves Cr2O3 passive layer)
foodMatrices.organolepticRisk: Noticeable astringent metallic sharpness if reduced in scratched or economy steel
foodMatrices.description: A highly concentrated acidic reduction utilizing fresh lemon juice and wine vinegar. At pH 2.3, the concentration of active hydronium ions is nearly 40 times higher than in tomato sauce. Hydronium ions rapidly reduce chromium(III) oxide into soluble Cr3+ cations, triggering rapid metal ion dissolution if boiled for more than 30 minutes.

foodMatrices.name: Acidulated Bone Broth (Simmered with Apple Cider Vinegar)
foodMatrices.chelationPotency: Very High (Prolonged 8 to 24-hour cook duration compensates for milder pH)
foodMatrices.organolepticRisk: Broth accumulates high cumulative metal dose over prolonged heating times
foodMatrices.description: Simmering marrow bones for 8 to 24 hours with added apple cider vinegar to extract collagen and minerals. Although pH 4.1 is milder than pure tomato sauce, the sheer duration of thermal contact (480–1440 minutes) combined with gelatin and amino acid histidine complexes drives cumulative nickel and chromium migration to high levels.

foodMatrices.name: Spicy Beef Chili with Tomatoes & Peppers
foodMatrices.chelationPotency: Moderate (Lipid coating on pan walls provides partial barrier against direct acid attack)
foodMatrices.organolepticRisk: Low organoleptic impact; rich beef fats and cumin mask minor metallic tones
foodMatrices.description: Chili contains tomato paste and onions at pH 4.6, but the presence of rendered beef tallow and vegetable oil coats the stainless steel surface with a temporary hydrophobic barrier, slowing down acid ion diffusion compared to thin aqueous sauces.

foodMatrices.name: Boiling Salted Water (Pasta / Vegetables)
foodMatrices.chelationPotency: Negligible (Near-neutral pH does not chemically chelate metal ions)
foodMatrices.organolepticRisk: Zero metallic flavor; safe for all users except in cold-salt pitting scenarios
foodMatrices.description: Standard boiling water with 1% dissolved culinary table salt. At pH 6.8, hydronium concentration is virtually zero, meaning chemical leaching of nickel and chromium is negligible (<1.0 µg/kg), provided salt was added after reaching a boil to avoid pitting corrosion.

foodMatrices.name: Acidic Sauce Stored Overnight in Stainless Pot (Cold Fridge)
foodMatrices.chelationPotency: Moderate-High (Cold temperature slows diffusion, but 24-hour static contact promotes leaching)
foodMatrices.organolepticRisk: Sauce absorbs metallic flavor along pot waterline due to differential oxygen aeration cells
foodMatrices.description: Leaving leftover tomato sauce or curry inside the cooking pot in the refrigerator for 24 hours. While refrigeration at 4°C reduces Arrhenius kinetic reaction rates, the static contact between stagnant acidic liquid, atmospheric oxygen, and the metal meniscus creates differential aeration corrosion cells, steadily leaching nickel and chromium into the stored food.

coeCmRes20139Ni.name: Council of Europe CM/Res(2013)9 Nickel SRL
coeCmRes20139Ni.scope: Specific Release Limit for food contact metals in the European Union
coeCmRes20139Ni.clinicalContext: Cookware exceeding 140 µg/kg of nickel in standard citric acid tests is legally non-compliant for sale in the EU.

coeCmRes20139Cr.name: Council of Europe CM/Res(2013)9 Chromium SRL
coeCmRes20139Cr.scope: Specific Release Limit for total chromium in the European Union
coeCmRes20139Cr.clinicalContext: Sets the European ceiling for total chromium migration to ensure culinary food contact safety.

efsaTdiNickel.name: EFSA Tolerable Daily Intake (TDI) for Nickel
efsaTdiNickel.scope: European Food Safety Authority 2020 Updated Scientific Opinion on Nickel in Food
efsaTdiNickel.clinicalContext: Establishes safe lifetime daily intake for the general population. Exceeding this benchmark increases risks of reproductive toxicity and systemic hypersensitivity.

snasAllergyThreshold.name: Systemic Nickel Allergy Syndrome (SNAS) Clinical Threshold
snasAllergyThreshold.clinicalContext: For the 10%–15% of the female population and 2%–4% of males sensitized to nickel, oral ingestion of as little as 20–50 µg of bioavailable nickel can trigger systemic flare-ups, dyshidrotic eczema, urticaria, fatigue, and irritable bowel symptoms.

scientificGuidelines.title: The First-Use Vinegar Boil Passivation Protocol
scientificGuidelines.description: Never cook tomato sauce or acidic food in a brand-new stainless steel pan immediately after unboxing. Fill the pan with a 50/50 mixture of water and distilled white vinegar, bring to a gentle boil for 15 minutes, discard the liquid, and wash with mild dish soap. This accelerated passivation wash removes microscopic manufacturing polishing residues, dissolves unbonded surface micro-burrs, and forces the uniform growth of a dense Cr2O3 oxide barrier before your first meal.

scientificGuidelines.title: The Rolling Boil Salting Rule
scientificGuidelines.description: Never add table salt to cold water in a stainless steel stockpot. Undissolved salt crystals sink to the bottom, where localized chloride concentrations (Cl⁻) dissolve the passive chromium oxide film and create irreversible microscopic pit corrosion within minutes. Always bring water to a rolling boil (100°C / 212°F) before adding salt, ensuring instantaneous crystal dissolution.

scientificGuidelines.title: Protocol for Nickel-Allergic & SNAS Individuals
scientificGuidelines.description: If you or a household member suffers from contact dermatitis, pompholyx, or Systemic Nickel Allergy Syndrome (SNAS), do not use 304 or 316 stainless steel for boiling acidic sauces. Transition to nickel-free AISI 430 stainless steel (18/0), vitreous enameled cast iron (Le Creuset/Staub), pure medical titanium cookware, or borosilicate glass pots.

scientificGuidelines.title: Never Store Acidic Foods Overnight in Stainless Steel
scientificGuidelines.description: Stainless steel is designed for dynamic cooking, not static chemical storage. Once your tomato sauce, chili, or citrus soup is cooked, immediately transfer leftovers into borosilicate glass or glazed ceramic storage containers before placing them in the refrigerator. Prolonged overnight static contact creates galvanic meniscus cells that degrade the metal finish and infuse meals with metallic ions.
